If you've spotted one German cockroach in your El Dorado kitchen, there's a good chance you're not just dealing with one. These roaches are the most common species found in homes and restaurants across Kansas, and they're notoriously hard to get rid of once they move in. Unlike the larger American cockroaches that wander in from outside, German cockroaches are homebodies — they live, breed, and hide almost exclusively indoors, which is exactly what makes them such a persistent problem.

## Why German Cockroaches Are Different

German cockroaches are small, usually under half an inch, light brown with two dark stripes running down their backs. What sets them apart from other roach species isn't their size — it's their reproduction rate. A single female can produce 30-40 eggs per egg case, and she can produce several egg cases in her lifetime. Do the math and one roach can turn into hundreds within a few months if conditions are right.

They also don't need much to survive. A few crumbs, a drip under the sink, a warm space behind the refrigerator — that's enough. They're drawn to kitchens and bathrooms specifically because those rooms offer the three things they need most: food, water, and warmth.

## Why Store-Bought Sprays Don't Work

We get this question a lot: "I sprayed under the sink and behind the fridge, why are they still here?" Here's the problem. German cockroaches don't live out in the open where a spray can reach them. They cluster in cracks, behind outlet covers, inside cabinet hinges, under appliances — spaces that are often less than an eighth of an inch wide. A surface spray kills what it touches, but it does nothing for the roaches hiding three inches back in a wall void.

Worse, some over-the-counter sprays actually make the problem harder to solve. Repellent-based sprays scatter roaches away from treated areas, pushing them deeper into walls and into neighboring rooms or units, which is especially bad news if you live somewhere like an apartment or duplex in [El Dorado](/el-dorado/).

## What Actually Works

Professional German cockroach control relies on a few things DIY approaches usually skip:

**Targeted gel baiting.** Instead of spraying surfaces, we place gel bait directly into cracks, crevices, and harborage points where roaches travel and hide. The roaches eat the bait, carry it back to the nest, and it spreads through the colony — including to roaches that never touched the bait directly. This is the single most effective tool against German cockroaches because it attacks the whole population, not just the roaches you can see.

**Inspection before treatment.** Every kitchen is laid out differently, and roach harborage spots vary from house to house. A real inspection means checking under the stove, behind the fridge, inside cabinet corners, around the water heater, and along baseboards — not just a quick walk-through.

**Growth regulators.** In heavier infestations, we also use insect growth regulators (IGRs) that interrupt the roach reproduction cycle, so even as adults die off, the next generation can't mature and breed.

**Follow-up.** One treatment visit rarely finishes the job on an established infestation. Egg cases that were laid before treatment will still hatch, so a second visit a few weeks later catches that new generation before it becomes a new colony.

## Sanitation Still Matters

Treatment does the heavy lifting, but a few habits make a real difference in keeping roaches from coming back:

- Wipe down counters and stovetops nightly, especially grease buildup
- Don't leave pet food out overnight
- Fix leaky faucets and dripping pipes under sinks
- Take trash out regularly instead of letting it sit
- Store dry goods like cereal and flour in sealed containers

None of this replaces treatment, but it removes the resources that let a surviving roach rebuild a colony.

## When to Call a Professional

If you're seeing roaches during the daytime, that's usually a sign the population has outgrown the available hiding spots — a strong indicator of a larger infestation. Other signs include a musty odor (German cockroaches produce a distinct smell when populations are high) and finding small dark droppings that look like coffee grounds or pepper flakes along baseboards and in cabinets.

At that point, DIY sprays and store-bought traps are usually playing catch-up. A professional treatment plan targets the whole colony at its hiding spots, not just the roaches wandering around in plain sight.
